description: After a major surge in dengue fever, the Brazilian city of Belém went all in to fight the virus. The result? They cut mosquito-borne diseases by 70% compared to the year prior: https://nyti.ms/3SNKhIO

comments.author: Jimmy Hayes
comments.text:
This is exactly why better health outcomes start upstream. With EK-TORUS + AFA Protocol, we’re focused on helping drug-discovery teams run larger, more stable computational workflows while adding verifiable provenance around how results are produced. The goal: more molecules explored, faster decisions, less rework

Test results at www.ektorus.com

comments.author: Cori Gorman
comments.text: The strongest lesson here is speed. Once transmission starts climbing, early intervention matters far more than reacting after hospitals are already under pressure.

comments.author: Nishant Kumar
comments.text:
This is a powerful reminder that the best solutions don’t just fight the symptoms—they change the conditions creating the problem.

Belém’s 70% reduction shows what can happen when science, data, government action, and community participation work together.

The bigger lesson goes beyond dengue: when we move from reacting to preventing, we don’t just solve today’s problem—we reduce the chances of facing the same problem tomorrow. 🌍👏

comments.author: Dong Cai Li
comments.text:
Persistent problems often survive because the conditions producing them remain intact.

Responding to outcomes may reduce the immediate damage.

Changing the underlying conditions reduces what the system can produce next.

Prevention becomes powerful when intervention moves upstream.

Change the conditions, and the outcomes can change with them.

comments.author: Narendra Kumar
comments.text: Bill Gates Absolutely right, Sir. 🙏 This is a great example of how the right technology, community participation and consistent execution can create a real impact. In my land acquisition work for renewable energy projects, I also see that long-term results depend not only on identifying the right land, but on understanding the surrounding challenges and working on them systematically. When technology and people work together with the right approach, even complex challenges can become opportunities for sustainable progress. 🇮🇳

comments.author: Sandy "UNIQUE" Johnson-Grimes
comments.text: That’s a powerful example of how focused public health action can make a measurable difference. It’s encouraging to see cities turning innovation and coordinated prevention efforts into real progress against mosquito-borne diseases.

comments.author: Smita Das Jain
comments.text: Mosquito-borne diseases require adaptive solutions. Brazil’s experience shows what becomes possible when innovation meets coordinated public-health action.

comments.author: Adam Wang
comments.text:
Looks like the mosquitoes finally met a team they couldn’t outsmart. 🦟😄
 A 70% reduction is an incredible achievement — a great reminder that public health solutions can make a real difference when science, strategy, and community action come together.

comments.author: Flor de María Cisneros
comments.text: Una iniciativa muy interesante. La prevención y la participación activa de la comunidad son fundamentales para enfrentar enfermedades transmitidas por mosquitos como el dengue. Este tipo de experiencias demuestra la importancia de combinar ciencia, políticas públicas y compromiso ciudadano para proteger la salud colectiva

comments.author: Samuel Ajiboyede
comments.text: This 70% reduction in Belém highlights what focused public health efforts achieve, Bill. The real challenge is sustaining it.
